a:
This calendar is the graduate dissertation of an expert in Homo sapiens culture and society. 

Homo sapiens was a species of literate primate on the planet Sol-3.

Because this species lived so long ago, and so far away, we have to make some educated guesses about their traditions based on the few facts we know for certain.

Fortunately, we have strong evidence that humans shared Sol-3 with at least 6,760 other mammals.

And we know that they used a calendar of 365 days and 12 months.

It stands to reason that they would designate specific days to celebrate each of their fellow-mammals.

q: Why are some kinds of mammals celebrated only during certain months?
a:
Given our fragmentary knowledge of human society, we only know two things for certain: Groundhog Day is on February 2, and Mole Day is on October 23. 

It can't be a coincidence that there are 12 major groups of mammals and 12 months of the human year.

From these and other observations, the humans' likely system of mammal celebrations falls into place.

Given their well-known self-regard, humans would naturally place their own lineage -- apes, monkeys, lemurs, colugos, and treeshrews -- at the top of the year. We also know that to ring in the new year, humans would pack as many of themselves as possible in a special city known for its mythical giant gorilla.
We know that Groundhog Day was February 2, therefore all other rodents must share this month, from the mighty capybara to the pygmy jerboa.

We know that many humans celebrated rabbits and hares during this time of year, for reasons that are lost to time. We also know that they often rang in the month of March with a special holiday called "Leap Day."
We know that egg-worship was common across many human cultures during this time of year. What better time to celebrate the egg-laying platypus and its various echidna relatives?
Motherhood was widely celebrated during May, and what says motherhood more than a helpless joey safely tucked away in the pouch of a kangaroo, koala, or sugar glider?
June was a time for celebrating difference as something to be proud of, thus we can confidently conclude that this was the time to celebrate tenrecs, elephant shrews, and aardvarks.

We know that the month of July was associated with patriotic celebrations, chief among them a contest over who could consume the most hot dogs in a short period of time. 

This most sacred of rituals took place near a special avenue named after the Mermaid, also known as the Sea Cow, a close relative of elephants and hyraxes as well.

Two pieces of evidence make this relationship incontrovertible: 

First, August is linked to Sirius, the Dog Star, and thus the Dog Days of Summer.

Second, August is the month that a culturally significant film was first released, emphasizing lions and tigers and bears.

And presumably also pangolins. Oh my are they close relatives.
This was a time to celebrate time off from honest labor. What better symbol of relaxation than the sloth, along with its relatives the anteaters and armadillos?
We know that Mole Day was October 23, therefore all true moles must share this month, along with their relatives the hedgehogs and true shrews.
There is ample evidence that this month was ushered in by an all-night celebration of bats and other creatures of the night.
Something big was going on with reindeer. We're not sure what, but surely this month celebrated all hoofed mammals, and their close relatives the whales.

q: How do we know exactly when to celebrate each mammal species?
a:
It would have been impossible to know, but Mole Day gave us the key.

Not only is Mole Day known to have been celebrated on October 23, we also know the time of day was precisely 6:02.

Surely the mole species in question was the Japanese mole, with the scientific name Mogera wogura.

The "W" in "wogura" is the 23rd letter of the alphabet, revealing why Mole Day was celebrated on the 23rd day of October.

It follows naturally that species beginning with "A" were celebrated on the 1st day of the month, "B" on the 2nd day, etc., and "Z" on the 26th day. 

Species beginning "AA" would be celebrated on the 27th, "AB" on the 28th, etc., through "AE" on the 31st.

The remaining letters of the species name reveal the proper time of day to celebrate.

For example, the "OGURA" in "Wogura" adds up to 15+7+12+18+1 = 62. The sixth hour and the second minute, or 6:02.

It's simplicity itself!
